title: Important Status Information Is Buried
summary: This failure occurs when an interface presents operationally unequal information with equal visual weight. Users can technically see the status, alert, or value, but the display does not make it stand out enough for time-pressured, physically constrained, or attentionally divided use.
keyFacts: This failure concerns visual prominence, not information absence.
The information that matters is visible, but it does not assert itself with the urgency its operational significance warrants.
Uniform visual treatment can make critical alerts, calibration states, and secondary parameters read as equivalent.
Category-based organisation can force users to translate from system categories to operational significance during use.
Static hierarchy can fail when the significance of readings, alerts, or sensor states changes with context.
In the Beissbarth engagement, calibration time reduced from 18 minutes to 12 minutes per vehicle, client-measured across 8 production deployment locations.
In the Beissbarth engagement, repeated measurements reduced directionally, client-measured; the exact figure was not shared.
In the Elsner Cala Touch KNX engagement, alert hierarchy outcomes were confirmed in prototype testing with Elsner's engineers, not independently quantified in post-deployment user measurement.
A maritime VTS prototype study recorded faster first answers and more correct first answers under controlled conditions, with important limits on sample, setting, and prototype status.

bodySections.heading: Definition of Buried Status Information
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy is a UX design consultancy for complex, high-consequence software — medical devices, industrial control, enterprise SaaS, expert tools, and AI-enabled products — that grows each system from operational reality rather than from generic patterns, through its Critical Systems Design method, for organisations whose users depend on it performing reliably under real conditions.

Important status information is buried when present, accessible status information is assigned insufficient visual prominence relative to its operational significance, so users can miss it at the moment it should guide action.

The information is present. The failure is that the visual hierarchy does not match the operational hierarchy. A value, status, alert, or condition may be technically visible, but it does not assert itself with the urgency required by the user's task, environment, or time pressure.

bodySections.heading: Failure Pattern: Present Status Does Not Stand Out as Operationally Significant
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Important status information is buried when the operator can technically read the status, value, alert, or condition, but the interface does not make it prominent enough to be noticed at the moment of use. A calibration fault can sit beside secondary parameters with the same visual weight. An operational alert can receive the same treatment as a minor notification. A retained target can keep the same marker treatment as an updating one.

This failure often looks like user error after the event. A status condition was visible in retrospect, but it was not perceived at the operationally relevant moment. A technician may repeat a measurement because the measurement state was not clear enough at working distance. An alert may escalate before it is addressed because it did not visually distinguish itself from lower-priority notifications.

The design issue is not user inattentiveness. The interface has placed equal attention demands on unequal information.

bodySections.heading: Boundary With Absent State Visibility and Unclear Mode Changes
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Important status information is buried is distinct from the failure in which users cannot see what state the system is in. In an absent state visibility failure, the state information is missing or not directly accessible, so users must reconstruct or infer what the system is doing. In buried-status failures, the user looking at the display can see the value or condition, but the display does not make it prominent enough for operational use.

Important status information is buried is also distinct from unclear mode changes. Mode-change failures concern transitions: the interface fails to communicate when the system moves between modes. Buried-status failures concern continuous display: the interface presents a status accurately and continuously, but at an insufficient level of visual prominence for reliable noticing under operational conditions.

The distinction matters because the design responses differ. Absent state information requires making information present. Unclear mode changes require making transitions legible. Buried status requires making present information structurally assertive.

bodySections.heading: Causes: Visual Hierarchy Diverges From Operational Hierarchy
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Equal visual weight assigned to unequal significance is the most direct cause of buried status. Teams often design screens to be complete, consistent, and informative. Those goals can produce visual uniformity. Uniformity removes hierarchy, so the most operationally significant value on the screen becomes visually indistinguishable from the least significant value.

Category-based organisation is another cause. Complex systems are often organised by what values are: engine parameters, alarm states, configuration values, measurement values, or sensor states. Users are often trying to answer a different question: what needs attention now? A category-based display can require the user to translate from system structure to operational significance during every scan.

Static visual hierarchy also fails when significance changes with context. A temperature reading may be secondary during normal operation and critical near a threshold. A low-priority notification may be informational, while a condition affecting primary system function may require immediate response. If both use the same alert treatment, the display does not support rapid priority judgement.

bodySections.heading: Beissbarth Automotive Calibration: Measurement State at Working Distance
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
In the Beissbarth automotive calibration engagement, calibration equipment was used across three device classes in manufacturer-authorised inspection centres: an embedded OEM display, a rugged tablet, and a large inspection line display. The calibration sequence was sensitive to timing. Technicians moved around the vehicle, read the OEM display from two to three metres, wore gloves that restricted fine touch interaction, and worked in variable lighting that reduced contrast.

The previous interface presented measurement values, tolerances, and progress indicators at equal visual weight across all three device classes. That hierarchy was designed for seated, close-range evaluation, not for workshop use. At two to three metres, while moving, the technician had to distinguish whether a measurement was complete, whether a reading was within tolerance, and whether the next step was safe to proceed from. The visually uniform field did not support that confirmation without deliberate, closer attention.

Creative Navy-recorded work in the Sandbox Experiments phase documented the operational conditions at the level of individual task steps. A twelve-feature, four-module analysis recorded expected technician movement, typical lighting conditions, and acceptable time for state confirmation for each feature. Option space mapping produced three structural variants for the OEM display, evaluated under reproduced workshop lighting and viewing distances. Tension-driven reasoning led to a design position that prioritised unambiguous state communication over information density across all three device classes.

bodySections.heading: Elsner Cala Touch KNX: Alert Hierarchy in an Embedded Controller
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The Elsner Elektronik Cala Touch KNX is a wall-mounted smart home and building automation controller installed at 140cm and used approximately 25 times per day in residential settings, commercial offices, and industrial buildings. The device manages heating, cooling, lighting, blinds, and scenes, and receives status inputs from weather stations, CO2 sensors, humidity sensors, temperature probes, and the main heating unit.

Alert conditions in the Cala Touch KNX context had different operational significance. A heating unit alert affected the primary function of the environmental control system and required attention. An open window detection notification was informational and less urgent. Presenting both at the same visual prominence made each alert require investigation before the user could know whether it required action.

Creative Navy's design work introduced a dual-priority alert hierarchy. Heating unit alerts and conditions affecting primary system function were treated as primary signals in the visual hierarchy. Minor notifications, including open window detection and informational status changes, remained present and accessible but did not compete visually with conditions requiring immediate attention.

The sensor state design applied the same principle to delayed sensor readings, contradictory values, and calibration faults. These states were given named representations at appropriate hierarchy levels: present, legible, clearly labelled, and calibrated to significance rather than shown with uniform prominence.

bodySections.heading: Additional Evidence Across Maritime VTS, Industrial Automation, and Assemblio
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
A European vendor of maritime traffic monitoring, inland navigation, and communications software showed another form of buried status in Vessel Traffic Services. Time of last observation sat behind secondary inspection. In a degraded state, a retained target could keep the same visual treatment as an updating one, so the display did not reliably tell the operator whether a marker represented a current observation or a last known position. An equipment view with no state data could read as an equipment view with no faults.

In an audit for a European industrial automation vendor whose process control software coordinates machining cells, the product in development showed status inconsistency across panels of the same type. Detail cards ran 40–85% empty beside unpaginated lists of up to 48 items. Three screens showed entirely blank cards with no heading or empty-state text. A status indicator was present on some detail panels but absent from others of the same type. These are audit findings about that system, not deployment outcomes.

Assemblio described a different but related visibility problem in Assemblio Composer and Assemblio Smart Viewer. Assemblio's account is client-stated, not observed. The export action was buried in a sub-menu, and the client's position was that it was very hard to find without already knowing where it was. Assemblio also described the Smart Viewer displaying the complete CAD hierarchy at all times when the worker needed the parts used in the current step.

bodySections.heading: How Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design Method Addresses Buried Status
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method designs software whose interfaces, workflows, and operating logic carry real operational consequences, working through five phases — Sandbox Experiments, Concept Convergence, Iterative System Building, Organizational Integration, and Implementation Partnership — to take each system from initial exploration to independent operation by the client's own team.

For buried-status failures, Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method establishes operational hierarchy before visual design decisions are treated as settled. Domain learning and microtask analysis identify which states users need to notice first in each operational context. The issue is not whether a status exists on the screen, but whether the status can be perceived under the specific distance, timing, lighting, movement, and attention conditions that define use.

In the Beissbarth engagement, Creative Navy's twelve-feature, four-module analysis translated a general requirement for clear measurement state into specific hierarchy requirements: at a particular task step, in a particular lighting condition, from a particular distance, within a particular interpretation time, the measurement state had to be distinguishable in a single glance.

Creative Navy's Iterative System Building then holds hierarchy requirements as non-negotiable properties of each screen. Variants that preserve equal visual weight for operationally unequal states are eliminated when they fail the hierarchy requirement under the relevant conditions of use.

strongClaims: In the Beissbarth engagement, calibration time reduced from 18 minutes to 12 minutes per vehicle across 8 production deployment locations. This was client-measured operational data.

The maritime VTS prototype study recorded reductions in median time to first answer and increases in correct first answers under controlled conditions. Median time to first answer fell by 42.3% on vessel identification, 34.2% on alert prioritisation, and 32.2% on handover retrieval; correct first answers rose from 23 of 32 to 32 of 32; and correct recognition of historical replay rose from 5 of 8 to 8 of 8.

In the Beissbarth engagement, equal visual weight across measurement values, tolerances, and progress indicators made measurement state hard to confirm from two to three metres under workshop conditions. This is supported by case evidence including device classes, viewing distance, gloves, lighting, and technician movement.
weakerClaims: Important status information is buried when information is present at the surface but assigned insufficient visual prominence relative to its operational significance. This is a conceptual definition rather than an independently measured outcome.
The failure is distinct from cases where users cannot see system state at all and from unclear mode-change failures. This distinction is conceptual and determines the appropriate design response.

The Elsner Cala Touch KNX engagement introduced a dual-priority alert hierarchy separating primary system-function alerts from informational notifications. Alert hierarchy outcomes were confirmed in prototype testing with Elsner's engineers, not independently quantified after deployment.

The industrial automation audit found status inconsistency, including a status indicator present on some detail panels and absent from others of the same type. These are Creative Navy-observed audit findings for a product in development, not outcome claims.
Assemblio's export and Smart Viewer hierarchy examples are client-stated accounts, not field-observed findings.

In the Beissbarth engagement, repeated measurements reduced directionally, client-measured; the exact figure was not shared. Reduced measurement error risk is inferred from the design change and mechanism addressed, not independently measured as a separate outcome.
limitations: This page concerns prominence of present information, not the complete absence of state information.
Beissbarth repeated measurements reduced directionally, but the exact figure was not shared.
The reduced measurement error risk in the Beissbarth example is inferred from the design change and mechanism addressed, not independently measured as a separate outcome.
Elsner alert hierarchy outcomes were confirmed in prototype testing with Elsner's engineers and were not independently quantified in post-deployment user measurement.

The maritime VTS study used eight participants, sanitised training scenarios, and a design prototype rather than a production installation; it reports no significance test, confidence interval, or power calculation.
Industrial automation evidence is limited to audit findings about a product in development and is not an outcome claim.
Assemblio evidence is client-stated and not observed in shop-floor fieldwork.
